extraction.name: MATH
extraction.description: A dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems with full step-by-step solutions written in LaTeX and natural language, designed to measure mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models across seven subjects and five difficulty levels.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.rai:dataCollection: MATH problems were collected from high school mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and others, sourced from online competition community archives such as Art of Problem Solving (AoPS).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Problems and solutions from high school math competitions (e.g., AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME) sourced from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests and originally created by the Mathematical Association of America (MAA).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions were consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers were forced to follow consistent formatting rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y and other fractions with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients encoded without multiplication symbols; multi-variable expressions in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order; equivalent fractions, parentheses encodings, and common numerical equivalents treated as identical; units allowed or omitted; and spaces ignored.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each problem is tagged by difficulty from 1 to 5 following AoPS standards (Level 1 being easiest, Level 5 hardest) and categorized across seven subjects (Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus). Final answers are wrapped and delimited using the \boxed{} command.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Models capable of solving these competition-level problems could have ramifications for cheating on homework or mathematics exams, but can help better forecast machine reasoning capabilities.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Current large language models exhibit very low accuracy (3.0% to 6.9%) and show severe overconfidence (AUROC of 68.8% for error detection). Scaling model parameters provides only slow improvements, requiring conceptual and algorithmic breakthroughs.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability, training models to generate step-by-step solutions and derivations, and testing reasoning capabilities. Not intended to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
